Abstract:

Acoustic metamaterials are specially engineered materials that can manipulate the propagation of sound waves through anomalous scattering, a phenomenon that is normally not possible in naturally occurring materials. The internal geometry of these materials plays a significant role in multiple-wave scattering (inside the material), thereby manipulating wave energy in a desired manner. These metamaterials show unnatural material characteristics such as negative density or negative bulk modulus, or both at the same time, during the propagation of the wave. While the passive type of acoustic metamaterials, where their acoustic property is frozen once they are fabricated, perform well at selective sound frequencies, the active ones exhibit more controllability in manipulating the acoustic waves, as the latter are dynamically reconfigurable. In this present work, as a starting phase of the research, different passive arrays of Helmholtz resonators (HR) are analysed to understand their acoustic behaviour in terms of transmission loss. A single-degree-of-freedom HR provides transmission loss (TL) at a specific frequency, namely, its resonant frequency. More HR modules in different planes, connected in parallel to a common duct, exhibit significant TL at approximately the same frequency. HRs in the same plane but connected opposite each other improve the array&rsquos sound absorption. It is also found that a gradual increase in the neck area of the HR modules significantly broadens the frequency bandwidth, but at the cost of a drastic deterioration in the array&rsquos noise-reduction capability.&nbsp Use of higher-degree-of-freedom oscillators in an array makes it useful for multi-frequency. However, significantly low TL is observed in these cases. The present work has applications in specially manufactured bricks or structural components, where ducts and cavities are arranged so as to create HR arrays within the material. These materials have application in low-frequency noise control, e.g, payload fairing, aero engine acoustic liners, and fuselage sidewall metamaterials, where components are exposed to short-duration low-frequency noises. As it has been found that the operation of these passive materials is limited to specific frequencies, research into making them reconfigurable poses a challenging engineering problem that will be addressed at a later stage.
